how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Asphalt sealcoating bid calculator

How much should I charge for sealcoating?

Enough to cover the gallons and the hours on that lot, not enough to match the cheapest postcard on the block. An 800 sq ft oxidized driveway with oil spots and forty feet of cracks is not the same job as a tight pad that was sealed last year, and a flat “cents per square foot” price cannot see the difference.

Open the free bid calculator

Price the first coat, then the second

Start with the square feet and how many coats you will actually put down. The first coat on oxidized asphalt drinks sealer — often around 80 to 90 square feet per gallon. The second coat is thinner because the first already filled the texture. Two coats is two crew passes, not a nicer name for one. A spray rig is faster labor than a squeegee; it is not free material.

Oil, cracks, and paint are not “included”

Oil spots need primer, not more sealer poured on top of a stain that will bleed through. Cracks are linear feet of filler and scrape time. Parking-lot striping is a second trade on the same visit: stalls, paint, and stencil time. If those lines are “included” in a $0.18-per-foot special on an 800 sq ft driveway, they are unpaid. That special is $144. The walk-away on a typical oxidized two-coat driveway with a short drive is often well above that.

The drive is a second job

Miles are a round trip. Eight miles at 35 mph is not “in the neighborhood”; it is almost half an hour on the clock before you blow off the lot. A trip / truck fee exists because the first hour of a tiny apron still required the tanker, the insurance, and the setup. If on-site time would land under your minimum, charge the minimum.

Then load the wage and keep a margin

A crew paid $24 often costs more than $31 once employer taxes, workers’ compensation (this is outdoor chemical work), liability, and paid time off are counted. Overhead sits on top of that direct cost. Margin is a share of the price the customer sees, not a markup you add last and forget. The walk-away number is total cost: below it the stop makes nothing, even before you pay yourself.

This is not a spec sheet

This is not a manufacturer yield, not a pavement-condition rating, and not a finding that a lot is ready to coat. Coal-tar and asphalt-emulsion sealers are not interchangeable, and some places ban one of them. The starting coverage figures are ballpark numbers so a contractor can see the shape of a bid. Replace them with yields from your own jobs, confirm condition on the lot, and have a qualified professional review anything that has to be signed or insured.

Price this lot in the calculator

Common questions

How much should I charge for sealcoating?

Charge the hours and gallons the stop will actually take — square feet times coats and coverage, plus oil-spot primer, crack fill, striping, travel, and a trip fee — then divide cost by one minus your target margin. A flat cents-per-square-foot price hides the difference between a tight driveway and an oxidized parking lot.

Why do two driveways of the same size bid so differently?

Condition, coats, oil, and cracks. Failing asphalt drinks the first coat. Two coats is two passes, not a nicer name for one. Oil spots need primer and cracks are linear feet. A neighborhood special that ignores those lines is how a crew works a half day for a one-hour price.

Is this a manufacturer yield or a pavement specification?

No. Starting coverage figures are editable ballpark numbers, not a product data sheet, a VOC approval, or a finding that any lot is ready to coat. Confirm sealer type, local rules, and condition on site.

No warranty. This free page is not legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a pavement specification, a VOC approval, or a product recommendation. Verify every figure against your own costs and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. FOR SEALCOATING CONTRACTORS

Bid the coats and the cracks, not the driveway special.

Price a sealcoating job the way the lot actually costs: each surface times coats and coverage, then oil-spot primer, crack fill, striping, the round trip, and the margin you intend to keep. You get the job price, what it works out to per square foot and per gallon, and the number below which the job loses money.

Where the coat hours go

Time your own crew and replace them. Confirm sealer type and local VOC rules yourself — this is not a product recommendation.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    Common questions

    What does this sealcoating estimate include?

    The price adds up sealer gallons for each surface by coats and coverage, oil-spot priming, crack fill by the foot, striping by the stall, an optional sand additive, a chosen add-on kit, setup and travel time, a trip fee, overhead, and your target margin — all from the surfaces, condition, and rates you enter, not a flat price list.

    Why does pavement condition change the price so much?

    Oxidized and failing pavement drinks the first coat — the calculator applies a coverage multiplier to the first-coat gallons for “good,” “oxidized,” and “failing” condition, so the same square footage on a badly oxidized lot uses more sealer and costs more than a recently sealed one. The second coat is not adjusted, since the first coat already did the drinking.

    How many square feet does a gallon of sealcoat cover?

    It depends on the surface preset the calculator uses to figure gallons: 90 sq ft/gal on the first coat and 120 sq ft/gal on the second for a residential driveway, 80/110 for a commercial parking lot, 85/115 for a basketball or play court, and 95/125 for a walkway or apron — a parking lot drinks more sealer per gallon than a driveway before condition even enters it. Condition then multiplies the first-coat number: on the default 800 sq ft, two-coat driveway at $4.25/gallon, “good” pavement uses 14.07 gallons ($59.81 in sealer) for a $362.27 job, “oxidized” uses 15.56 gallons ($66.11) for $371.93, and “badly oxidized/failing” uses 18.52 gallons ($78.70) for $391.23 — nearly 4.5 more gallons and about $29 more job price from condition alone, on the identical 800 square feet.

    Does it matter whether I squeegee or spray the job?

    Yes. Squeegee and spray application are each their own square-feet-per-crew-hour rate, so switching methods changes the apply hours for every surface without touching gallons, oil spots, crack fill, or striping, which price the same either way.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Usage counts are anonymous tallies of which features were used, stored locally, and a share link encodes only the quote fields in the page’s URL hash rather than sending anything to a server.

    What’s the difference between the job price and the walk-away price?

    The job price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, the trip fee, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — sealer, primer, crack filler, sand, striping paint, labor, and the trip — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all.

    Does this check whether a lot is ready to coat?

    No. This is not a pavement-condition assessment, a specification, or a finding that any lot is sound enough to seal. Oil spots, cracks, and stalls are quantities you count and enter yourself; whether the pavement underneath is fit to coat is a judgment call on site, not something this arithmetic can see.

vs-a-flat-per-square-foot-price.html.text:
← Asphalt Sealcoat Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-square-foot price

“35 cents a square foot, done” is not a price for a sealcoat job — it is a price for one pavement condition and one scope, quietly applied to every lot that gets called in.

What a flat per-square-foot price is

A flat per-square-foot price is the fastest way to quote a sealcoat job over the phone: multiply the square footage by a number and read it back. Customers shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's quote will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one kind of job — usually a residential driveway in ordinary condition, with few oil spots, little crack fill, and no striping — and then reused for every lot afterward, whether or not the next one is badly oxidized, carries oil spots and heavy crack fill, or needs stalls restriped.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each surface's square footage and coats, the pavement condition and application method, the oil spots to prime, the crack feet to fill, the stalls to stripe, and your own wage, payroll burden, materials, overhead, target margin, and travel. It prices the sealer gallons by condition and coats, adds priming, crack fill, and striping as their own lines, and returns the job price, the walk-away price, and the price per square foot — for this lot and this site, not a flat number for every job.

What a flat per-square-foot price doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same fee whether the pavement is a recently sealed lot or badly oxidized, failing asphalt that drinks nearly twice the first-coat sealer for the same area. Applies a coverage multiplier to first-coat gallons by condition (good, oxidized, failing), so worse pavement uses more sealer and costs more — the second coat is priced the same either way, since the first coat already did the drinking.
Has no line for oil spots at all — a lot with twenty of them gets the same quote as a clean one. Prices oil-spot priming by the spot, in both the primer gallons and the extra crew hours to prep them, before the coat goes down.
Quotes the same number for a lot needing 40 feet of crack fill and one needing 220, with no separate line for the filler or the labor. Prices crack fill by the linear foot in both filler material and crew hours, so a heavily cracked lot is never quoted at the light lot's price.
Has no line for restriping stalls after the coat — a lot with 24 stalls to paint gets the same number as one with none. Prices striping by the stall, in both paint and labor, as its own line rather than folding it into the square-footage number.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the price per square foot, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two 800 sq ft jobs, one flat price

Using this calculator's own shipped starting example:

An 800 sq ft residential driveway, in typical oxidized condition with 4 oil spots and 40 feet of crack fill, prices at $371.93 — $0.46 per square foot — on a job that costs $278.94 to run.

Take the same 800 square feet and make it a commercial parking lot instead — badly oxidized, failing condition that drinks more first-coat sealer, 20 oil spots to prime, 220 feet of crack fill, and 24 stalls to restripe — and the job costs $741.74 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $988.99: $1.24 per square foot, 2.66 times the easy job's price, on the identical square footage. Quoting the hard job at the easy job's flat $371.93 price prices it $369.82 below its own break-even cost — before counting the $617.07 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 25% target margin. Same square footage, same flat price, one lot that pays and one that loses money the moment the condition and the stalls show up.

Common questions

Why does a flat per-square-foot price get a sealcoating job wrong?

Because the cost driver is the condition and the scope, not the square footage. An 800 sq ft residential driveway in typical oxidized condition with a handful of oil spots and light crack fill needs one coat of sealer at a normal coverage rate and a short crew visit. An 800 sq ft commercial lot in badly oxidized, failing condition, with twenty oil spots to prime, 220 feet of crack fill, and 24 stalls to restripe, drinks more sealer per coat, adds priming and crack-fill and striping labor on top, and takes roughly three times as long -- on the identical square footage. A flat per-square-foot price charges both the same because it was priced on the area, not the condition or the scope.

What does a flat per-square-foot price usually leave out entirely?

Pavement condition, oil-spot priming, crack fill, and striping. A flat price has no line for oxidized or failing pavement drinking more sealer on the first coat than a recently sealed lot, no line for the primer and labor an oil spot needs before it can be coated at all, no line for crack fill by the linear foot, and no line for restriping stalls after the coat goes down. It also has no separate line for the extra crew hours all of that adds, since the flat number was set on square footage alone.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped starting example: an 800 sq ft residential driveway, in typical oxidized condition with 4 oil spots and 40 feet of crack fill, prices at $371.93, on a job that costs $278.94 to run -- $0.46 per square foot. The same 800 square feet as a commercial parking lot in badly oxidized, failing condition, with 20 oil spots, 220 feet of crack fill, and 24 stalls to stripe, costs $741.74 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices the job at $988.99 -- $1.24 per square foot, 2.66 times the easy job's price on the identical square footage. Quoting the hard job at the easy job's flat $371.93 price prices it $369.82 below its own break-even cost, before counting the $617.07 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 25% target margin. Same square footage, same flat price, one lot that pays and one that loses money the moment the condition and the stalls show up.

Is a flat per-square-foot price ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of similar jobs -- a residential driveway in ordinary condition, with few oil spots, little crack fill, and no striping -- a flat per-square-foot number can land close, because that is probably the job the price was set on. The risk is quoting a badly oxidized or failing lot, a job with heavy crack fill, or a lot that needs stalls restriped the same way sight unseen, because the price does not know the condition, the prep, or the scope until someone walks the site, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market, your sealer supplier's pricing, or your material costs. It takes the square footage and coats per surface, the pavement condition, application method, oil spots, crack feet, stalls to stripe, and your own wage, burden, travel, materials, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-square-foot price skips, not a market survey.

Open the Asphalt Sealcoat Bid Calculator to price your own job, or read the pricing walkthrough.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a pavement-condition assessment, a specification, or a finding that any lot is ready to coat. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, sealer yield, and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against any competing service — it is a static page describing the calculator's own worked example.

Free and open source. If it wins you a job, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-bitumio.html.text:

This calculator vs. Bitumio

Two different shapes: Bitumio is a subscription platform for running a paving company's estimating, scheduling, and job costing. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one lot or driveway cost, given its square footage, coats, and condition, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Bitumio is asphalt estimation and scheduling software built for the paving industry, aimed at asphalt maintenance contractors who focus on sealcoating, crack filling, striping, and repair work rather than new construction. It combines job estimating, scheduling, customer management, and job costing with integrated map measurement tools and QuickBooks integration. Its own marketing describes automated proposal generation and material-quantity calculations that factor in crack sizes, application method — spray versus squeegee — coverage rate, and waste. It is sold as an ongoing subscription with a free tier. Bitumio's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — paving-industry estimating and scheduling software, sold as a subscription with a free tier — are stated, and no dollar amount for Bitumio appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Bitumio does. It does not manage customer records, schedule crews, or integrate with accounting software, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one job's square footage, coat count, pavement condition, oil-spot priming, crack fill, sealer coverage rate and waste, loaded wage, payroll burden, materials, overhead, target margin, and travel, and turns that into the per-job price, the price per square foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.
